Hasbro’s New Playbook: More Magic, Fewer Big Bets

Weekly Digest
Hasbro’s New Playbook: More Magic, Fewer Big Bets
By Naavik •   November 8, 2026
Source:
Wizards of the Coast / Commander’s Herald
Hasbro’s brands span Monopoly, Dungeons & Dragons, Transformers, Nerf, and Play-Doh, but its latest results show how much its business and future now rest on Magic: The Gathering. In the
third quarter of 2026, tabletop revenue rose 39% to about $613M
, while Digital and Licensed Gaming grew 3% to roughly $134M. Management reported that
~$40M of Magic sales shifted forward from the fourth quarter
, boosting the comparison, but tabletop is still the clearest source of momentum.
In 2025, Hasbro as a whole generated $4.7B of revenue and $1.14B of adjusted operating profit. Wizards and Digital Gaming, the segment that includes Magic, Dungeons & Dragons, digital games, and related licensing,
generated about $2.2B of revenue and ~$1B of operating profit
(the vast majority of Hasbro’s operating profits). Consumer Products, its toys and licensed-products business,
grew revenue 4% to $828M in the latest quarter
, though tariff refunds supplied about $48M of the segment’s roughly $178M in adjusted operating profit.
Data:
Hasbro FY2025 Results
Magic has been the primary catalyst and can keep Hasbro growing for years. Its success also points toward a more profitable company built around complementary partners. Hasbro makes Magic and borrows other companies’ worlds to bring in fans; conversely, in video games, it increasingly supplies its IP while partners bring the development and operating expertise. As Hasbro centers its strategy more on where it offers the most value versus its partners, the company’s next phase partly depends on how well those IP crossovers sustain Magic and how well its video game strategy succeeds in creating hits at lower internal development costs while picking the right partners to license or co-develop the rest. That’s what we’ll explore today.
Why Magic Keeps Customers
A Final Fantasy fan now has several ways into Magic
. A newcomer could buy a starter kit containing two ready-to-play decks, choose a themed Commander deck for casual multiplayer, collect booster products, or play the set through Arena, Hasbro’s digital Magic game. For example, the
Limit Break ready-to-play deck features Cloud from Final Fantasy VII
, turning a recognizable character into a functional way to begin playing. These products serve players and collectors with different levels of interest rather than prescribing one route through the franchise.
Source:
Wizards of the Coast / Square Enix
For physical Universes Beyond products, Hasbro makes and sells Magic cards under licenses from outside rights holders. Those partners license familiar characters for a royalty fee, and Hasbro embeds them into the game, giving customers reasons to keep buying and playing. A player who starts with the
Cloud-led Limit Break Commander deck
can add eligible cards from later releases that meet its
color identity and other Commander requirements
, changing the strategy without replacing the entire deck. Since 2025,
main Universes Beyond booster sets have also been designed for Standard
, a format that periodically rotates older sets out of its eligible card pool. There are different paths to continued play, but most licensed additions add both a new entry point and an upsell path to keep playing.
Stores and organized play make that continuity useful. Hasbro’s
third-quarter presentation reports more than 13,000 Wizards Play Network stores, over one million unique organized-play players in 2025, and average player tenure above five years
. Management also said participation during the
first nine months of 2026 exceeded the full-year 2024 level by more than 40%
. Although this comparison does not represent conventional YoY growth, it indicates increased participation in Magic’s organized-play infrastructure. Stores give each release somewhere to be discovered, played, and revisited.
Universes Beyond also works when some customers never move beyond the franchise that first attracted them to Magic. A Final Fantasy collector who buys cards as character objects can still be valuable, just as
Pokémon enables collecting and trading favorite cards alongside casual and competitive play
. Obviously, converting a new buyer into a long-term Magic player is ideal, but it is not the only acceptable commercial outcome. Hasbro can serve collectors, active players, and customers who both collect cards and play, provided the products remain compelling and the release cadence does not exhaust them.
What the Growth Proves
In the latest earnings call, management said
sales from previously released sets — its “backlist” — had already exceeded the prior full-year level and were growing faster than new-release sales
, even though new releases still supplied most revenue. Foundations, Final Fantasy, and The Lord of the Rings were among the quarter’s strongest backlist performers, showing that demand can persist beyond launch across both Magic-owned and licensed worlds. Rising organized-play participation adds to that positive picture. Hasbro has not disclosed how many newly acquired crossover customers explore other franchises or how long they remain engaged, but some newcomers are likely to become repeat buyers as they discover the wider game.
Magic’s sales growth can come from several obvious yet valuable sources. A strong license may attract new buyers or franchise-specific collectors, existing players may spend more, and premium products may improve the sales mix.
Larger initial production runs
also help Hasbro meet demand it previously could not fill. Royalty payments reduce returns on each licensed product, but the additional sales can more than compensate. The strategy appears to be working: as noted earlier,
Wizards’ 2025 operating profit grew 59% to $1B
, while revenue increased 45%. That is segment profit, including businesses beyo
